title: KV cache reuse / eviction / paging / memory-bandwidth investigation
content:
Summary:

This document captures the investigation into KV cache behavior observed on 80B LLM load profiles (seq_len=2048, batch mix with short/long tails). Goal: quantify reuse rates, measure eviction pressure & paging, and determine whether host/GPU memory bandwidth or eviction policy is the dominant limiter for p99 latency and sustained throughput.

Background / motivation:
- Several customer workloads started hitting tail latency regressions in the last two weeks on Dedicated clusters.
- Symptoms: p99 latency spike (+35–80ms) under steady-state token generation with mixed prompt lengths; throughput dropped ~10% on some nodes.
- Hypothesis (initial): high KV cache churn leads to device-host paging and additional memcpy overhead; alternate hypothesis is PCIe/NVLink memory bandwidth saturation from frequent KV loads.

Environment / baseline:
- Model: rw-80b-v1 (dense attention), quantized int8 in inference pipeline.
- HW: A100-80GB (PCIe and NVLink pool mixes across clusters).
- Runtime: serving-runtime v1.12.3 (baseline metrics), CUDA 12.1, ROCtools disabled.
- Workload: synthetic replay of production traces (June->March mix) with token generation mix: 70% short (<256), 20% mid (256-1024), 10% long (1024-2048).
- Measurement tools: perf (user/kernel), nvprof / Nsight Systems sampling, in-house telemetry (kv-cache hit/miss counters, eviction counters, page-fault counters), and BPF-based memcpy sampling.

Experiment matrix (high level):
1) Baseline (current policy: LRU-ish segmentation, max_kv_mem_ratio=0.6)
2) High-residency (pin more KV: max_kv_mem_ratio=0.85)
3) Aggressive-evict (reduce memory cap to 0.45)
4) Prefetch/pro-active-keep (keep recent N prefixes pinned)
5) Bandwidth-limited (artificially throttle memcpy to emulate lower PCIe/NVLink)
6) No-paging mode (run bigger on-GPU-only model config to avoid host->device paging)

Key metrics collected per run:
- KV reuse rate (fraction of requests that hit existing KV pages per token)
- Eviction rate (# evictions per 1M token steps)
- Paging bytes/sec (host->device memcopy) and memcpy latency distribution
- Device memory bandwidth utilization (GB/s) – from nvlink/perf counters
- p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec throughput
- CPU syscall overhead (percentage of time in memcpy syscalls / driver)

Top-level findings:
- Reuse rate correlates strongly with tail latency: reuse >85% -> stable p99; reuse 60-75% -> clear p99 tail increases.
- Most p99 spikes align with high short-lived eviction bursts when long requests interleave with many short requests (mixed trace).
- Paging traffic (host->device memcpy) scales superlinearly with eviction rate; runs with eviction_rate > 1k evictions/1M tokens saw paging bytes/sec increase 3–5x vs baseline.
- Device-to-host memory bandwidth (NVLink) was under nominal sustained peak; the bottleneck was memcpy short bursts and driver/PCIe latency rather than raw bandwidth saturation.
- Artificial bandwidth throttling showed throughput drop but did not reproduce p99 spikes of the same shape – indicating latency of page transfers and serialization in memcpy paths is the issue, not just bandwidth.
- Prefetch/pinning strategy (experiment 4) gave the best p99 improvement for mixed traces: p99 reduced by ~40ms (median of three runs) and tokens/sec recovered to within 3% of baseline.

Detailed notes / evidence:
- Baseline run (3x): reuse_rate=71%, eviction_rate=1.2k/1M, paging_bytes=220MB/s peaks, p99=420ms. CPU memcpy syscalls accounted for ~12% of wall time in p99 tail samples.
- High-residency run: reuse_rate=89%, eviction_rate=140/1M, paging_bytes=45MB/s, p99=370ms – modest improvement but cost is higher GPU memory pressure causing fewer concurrent pipelines on some nodes.
- Aggressive-evict run: reuse_rate=58%, eviction_rate=1.8k/1M, paging_bytes=420MB/s peaks, p99=495ms – worst-case scenario; sharp latency spikes when small long-running sequences caused mass evictions.
- Prefetch/pinning run (heuristic: keep top-10k recent prefixes pinned per model instance): reuse_rate=82%, eviction_rate=520/1M, paging_bytes=110MB/s, p99=380ms.
- No-paging run (large on-GPU config): reuse_rate~87%, paging_bytes~5MB/s, p99=360ms but only possible with <70% concurrency due to memory; implies tradeoff between concurrency and latency.

Profiling observations (hot paths):
- Hot functions: kv_lookup(), kv_evict_work(), device_memcpy_async (driver), post_copy_sync; many p99 stacks end up in driver synchronization after memcpy (cudaStreamSynchronize / cuMemcpy).
- BPF traces show many small (<64KB) host->device memcopies; each has non-trivial launch overhead (~10-60us) and high variance which adds to latency tail.
- Bandwidth counters on NVLink show spikes but average utilization ~40–55% during the worst runs. Peak bursts correlate with eviction bursts.

Hypotheses (revised):
- Primary cause: eviction churn producing many small, serialized host->device memcpy operations with high per-op overhead and blocking points (cudaStreamSynchronize calls), leading to p99 tail.
- Secondary: when eviction rate is high, overall paging bytes/sec increases which can compete for PCIe/NVLink in tight bursts causing transient queuing.

Recommended mitigations (short-term):
1) Coalesce memcopies: group small KV page transfers into larger batched transfers when possible (runtime-level coalescing) – expected p99 drop 20–50ms based on emulation.
2) Reduce synchronization: move to more asynchronous copy patterns and avoid sync points per small page; use CUDA graph captures or pipelined streams.
3) Heuristic pinning: adopt a conservative pinning default for mixed-workload clusters (e.g., max_kv_mem_ratio bump to 0.75 for Dedicated tier with memory headroom) and expose as a runtime knob.
4) Eviction policy tweak: move from purely LRU segmentation to frequency-aware eviction (LFU/LRU hybrid) to keep high-reuse prefixes longer.
5) Instrumentation: increase sampling for memcpy sizes and queue latency in production telemetry to validate in wider fleet.

Longer-term work / experiments:
- Implement memcopy coalescer in serving-runtime and run AB test on Dedicated pool (SERV-1423).
- Evaluate moving cold pages to a compressed on-host layout to reduce bytes transferred per eviction.
- Explore host-side page cache prefetcher using workload predictors (ML-lite heuristic) to reduce miss latency in mixed tails.

Risks / tradeoffs:
- Pinning more KV reduces eviction/paging but increases per-node memory footprint -> lowers concurrency; need pricing/throughput tradeoff analysis.
- Coalescing copies increases latency for some single large-request cases if not carefully scheduled; must tune thresholds.

Action items (owners):
- Priya: PR for coalescing prototype + microbench harness (due 2026-04-26).
- Liam: add memcpy size/queue latency metrics to telemetry pipeline and dashboard (due 2026-04-19).
- Sophia: prototype LFU hybrid eviction policy in sim harness and validate reuse curves (due 2026-05-03).
- Ethan: run Dedicated pool canary with conservative pinning (0.75) and collect fleet metrics (start 2026-04-20).

Appendix / quick logs:
- baseline_run_2026-04-08.log: (attached in artifacts) key lines: "evictions: 1203/1M tokens, avg_memcpy_us: 32, memcpy_count: 12k"
- nvlink_counters_2026-04-09.csv: peaks @ 420GB/s for <100ms bursts; sustained avg 180GB/s (per-socket aggregated).

Open questions / unknowns:
- Are some model architectures (sparsity patterns / attention layouts) more eviction-sensitive? Need to run on rw-13b/33b to compare.
- Can we leverage CUDA graph or GPUDirect RDMA to reduce copy sync overhead without major refactor?

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working doc; data attachments and raw traces are in the linked GitHub PR and Confluence page. Please comment if you have alternative eviction heuristics or concerns about memory footprint tradeoffs.

End.
